_about: Phrase banks for the long weekly story (see public/js/narrator-offline.js). One line is picked at random and lines used recently are skipped. Tokens: {J} player, {M}/{Mf} manager, {club}, {opp}, {score}, {comp}, {venue}, {MUM} {DAD} {SIB} {SIBr} {BF} {BFf} {BFjob} {Pf} partner, {JR} {OUT} journalist/outlet, {CAP} {CAPl} captain, {PRES} {PRESl} president, {T} ally teammate, {R} rival teammate, random words {PLACE} {FOOD} {DAY} {WEATHER} {SHOW} {HOBBY} {CAR} {GIFT}, {month}, {age}. Add lines freely.

match: Matchweek. The training ground is quieter than usual, the jokes a little shorter. {WEATHER} over the stadium on the morning of the game.
The week bends towards one thing: the match. Everything else — meals, sleep, phone calls — is arranged around it.
{month}, and the fixtures come thick and fast. {J} has learnt to recognise the particular silence of a matchday morning.
Monday is recovery, Tuesday is work, Wednesday is shape, Thursday is set-pieces, and then it is game day. {J} could recite the rhythm in his sleep.
A matchweek in {WEATHER}. The kit man lays out the shirts in silence; {J}'s number is on the hook nearest the door.
The team bus smells of liniment and nerves. {J} sits in the same seat as always, three rows from the back, headphones on.
On the morning of the match {J} eats exactly what the nutritionist says and nothing else, which for him is an act of heroism.
Matchday. {J} wakes before the alarm, which is either a very good sign or a very bad one.
quiet: No fixture this week. The training ground belongs to the coaches, the cones and the long, repetitive work nobody films.
A week without a match always feels longer. {J} fills it with drills, video, ice baths and too many thoughts.
{month} drags. {WEATHER} all week, and the only thing on the schedule is work.
A quiet week, which in football means a week where everything that matters is invisible.
The calendar is empty and the body is grateful. {J} spends the week rebuilding the small things.
No match, no headlines — or so {J} thinks on Monday morning.
International breaks, cup gaps, fixture holes: whatever it's called, it's a week of work in the shadows.

Focused: {J} feels focused: one session at a time, one meal at a time.
His head is clear this week, the noise turned down to a hum.
He's in that rare state where nothing distracts him.
Determined: There is something hard in {J}'s jaw this week. He wants something and he knows it.
{J} arrives first and leaves last. Nobody has to ask why.
Determination looks boring from the outside: extra reps, early nights. {J} is very boring this week.
Motivated: {J} is hungry. Every drill feels like an audition.
Motivation is cheap, they say. {J} has plenty this week anyway.
He can't sit still. Every session feels like a chance.
OnFire: {J} is flying. Everything he touches seems to work, and he's stopped questioning why.
Confidence is a drug and {J} is high on it this week.
Teammates have started passing to him in training just to see what he'll do.
Confident: {J} walks a little taller this week.
He's playing without fear — the best way to play.
The doubts are quiet. {J} enjoys the silence.
Anxious: {J} sleeps badly. His mind runs the same three thoughts on a loop at 3am.
There's a knot in his stomach that won't untie, no matter how many sessions he does.
He checks his phone too often and hates what he reads.
Frustrated: {J} is frustrated, and it leaks out in small ways: a kicked ball, a short answer, a slammed locker.
Nothing seems to go his way and he's started taking it personally.
{J} trains angry. Coaches love it until he catches someone late.
Broken: {J} feels broken. Getting out of bed is a decision, not a habit.
Some weeks you just survive. This is one.
The light has gone out of him, and everyone around him can see it.
Lost: {J} feels lost — in the squad, in the city, in his own head.
He doesn't know what he's working towards anymore, only that he has to keep working.
There's a fog around everything this week.
Homesick: {J} misses home with a physical ache: the food, the noise, his mother's voice in the next room.
Every video call home ends with a silence neither side wants to fill.
Angry: {J} is angry and doesn't fully know at whom.
The fury is useful in tackles and dangerous everywhere else.
Numb: {J} goes through the motions. He feels nothing much, which scares him more than feeling bad.
Numb is a strange place: no highs, no lows, just the next session.
Relieved: A weight has lifted and {J} can breathe properly again.
Relief makes him generous: he buys the whole kit room coffee.

starter: {J} is a first-choice name now. The pressure has changed shape: it's no longer 'will I play?' but 'how well?'.
His place in the eleven feels secure — for now. In football, 'for now' is the only kind of secure.
Starting every week brings a new kind of tiredness, and {J} wouldn't trade it for anything.
rotation: {J} is in and out of the side. Every chance has to count double.
Rotation means living on the edge of the eleven: some weeks in, some weeks watching.
He's close. Close enough to taste it, far enough to hurt.
bench: The bench is where {J} lives at the moment. He warms up properly every time anyway.
{J} has memorised the pattern of the dugout roof. He'd rather not have.
Minutes are scarce. {J} treats every training session like a cup final, because it's the only stage he gets.
outcast: {J} trains with the reserves now. Nobody says the word 'outcast'. Nobody has to.
His name isn't on the team sheets pinned to the dressing-room wall. He checks anyway.
The first team trains on pitch one. {J} is on pitch four, with the kids and the forgotten.

hard: {J} asked for a hard week and gets one: double sessions, sprint ladders, finishing until his legs scream. The fitness coach writes 'good' on his sheet, which is the highest praise he gives.
A brutal week by choice. {J} stays out after every session, running the hill behind the training ground until the light goes.
The hard week bites. By Thursday {J} is limping up the stairs to the canteen, and smiling about it.
Extra gym, extra shooting, extra video. {J} goes to bed at nine every night because his body gives him no choice.
He trains like a man trying to outrun something. The coaches love it; the physios are less sure.
balanced: A sensible week on the training ground: sharp sessions, proper recovery, nothing wasted.
{J} does the work and nothing silly. Some weeks, the boring plan is the brave one.
Rondos, pattern play, a little finishing. A steady week of getting slightly better.
The week follows the plan to the minute. {J} has started to enjoy the rhythm of it.
Balanced work: one hard day, one tactical day, one light day. {J} feels fit and fresh.
light: A lighter week. {J} spends more time in the pool and the physio room than on the grass.
{J} manages his load: touches, short sprints, long stretches. The body says thank you.
Light training and early nights. {J} feels the springs come back into his legs.
He holds back this week, on purpose. It feels like cheating. It isn't.
rest: {J} takes proper rest: sleep, massage, a walk, {SHOW} on the sofa. Football will still be there on Monday.
Rest is training too, the sports scientist keeps saying. {J} finally believes him.
A week of nothing. It's harder than it sounds for someone who's never had a week of nothing.
{J} switches off. No gym, no clips. The fatigue drains out of him like water from a bath.
injured: The treatment room becomes {J}'s office: ice, lasers, resistance bands, and a physio who won't stop talking about her cat.
Rehab is a lonely job. While the squad trains outside, {J} counts reps in the gym with the blinds half down.
{J} watches training from the window of the physio room. He can hear the ball, which is worse than not hearing it.
Small victories: today he can walk without the brace. Tomorrow, maybe a jog.
The physios set him tiny goals and he smashes every one of them, then asks for more. They say no.
gain: The work pays off. The coaches' data shows it: {STATS}.
Small numbers, real progress: {STATS}. Nobody outside the building will notice yet.
Development report: {STATS}. {J} reads it twice and puts it in his drawer.

coachNote: On Thursday one of the assistant coaches pulls {J} aside to work on his first touch under pressure. Twenty minutes, one drill, a hundred repetitions.
{Mf} stops a session to move {J} two metres to the left. It changes everything. It's the kind of thing you only learn by being moved two metres to the left.
The goalkeeping coach uses {J} as target practice for crosses. He heads the ball so many times his forehead goes numb.
A veteran shows {J} a trick for holding off defenders: an arm, a hip, a lean. It's not in any textbook.
The analysts show {J} a clip of himself standing still while his man runs off him. Then they show it again. Then again.
In the small-sided game {J} is on the team that loses, and has to collect all the cones. Some traditions are sacred.
{CAP} stays behind to practise set-pieces with {J}. They barely speak. It's the best hour of the week.
The fitness coach introduces a new test. {J} finishes second and is annoyed about it for two days.
injuryLine: {J} sits in the physio room staring at the ceiling tiles, counting fixtures he will miss.
The walk from the treatment room to the car takes a long time on crutches.
He calls {MUM} from the car park and lies: 'It's nothing serious.' She knows.
The club doctor talks for five minutes. {J} only hears the number of weeks.
Teammates send messages: emojis, prayers, a meme. He reads them all at 2am.
recovered: {J} is back in full training after the {INJ}. The first sprint is tentative; the second is not.
The {INJ} is behind him. He celebrates his first full session like a goal.
Cleared. After the {INJ}, the grass smells better than he remembered.
Back with the group. The lads give him a round of applause and then immediately nutmeg him.

starter: The team sheet goes up on Friday and {J}'s name is in the eleven — and it's starting to look permanent.
{Mf} has seen enough: {J} is now a starter.
rotation: {J} is in the rotation now — in some weeks, out in others.
Squad status changes: {J} drifts into the rotation group.
bench: {J}'s name slides down the pecking order. The bench is his for now.
Squad status: back to the bench.
outcast: {J} is told to train with the reserves. It's the shortest meeting of his life.
Squad status: out of the picture. Nobody explains why. Nobody needs to.

home: The stadium is filling an hour before kick-off, and the noise carries all the way to the dressing room.
At home, in front of their own people. The walk out of the tunnel never gets old.
{opp} arrive with a plan to frustrate. The home crowd arrive with flags, drums and very little patience.
Home turf. {J} touches the grass on the way out, the way he always does.
A home game in {WEATHER}. The ultras have been singing since the gates opened.
away: Away at {opp}, where the home fans make it their personal mission to be heard.
The away dressing room is cramped and cold. Somebody's music is too loud. Nobody turns it down.
{opp} away. The bus has to crawl through a crowd of home fans banging on the windows.
On the road. The travelling supporters are few, but they've brought a drum.
An away day in {WEATHER}. The pitch is heavier than the one at home, and so are the legs.

Wbig: It's over by half-time. The second half is a procession, the away fans leaving in quiet clumps.
Every attack ends in a chance and most of the chances end in goals. One of those days.
The opposition collapse after the second goal. The rest is target practice.
Wclose: It's tight until the end — a scramble, a block, a goalkeeper stretching every inch — but the lead holds.
A nervy last ten minutes. The bench is on its feet for every throw-in. Then the whistle, and relief.
They don't play well, but they win. Coaches pretend to hate that sort of game.
One moment decides it, and it falls their way.
D0: Ninety minutes of chess with no checkmate. Both goalkeepers have quiet nights.
Chances are rare and nerves are high. Nobody finds the breakthrough.
A goalless draw that neither side quite deserves to win.
Dgoals: End to end. Every time one side scores the other answers, and nobody can kill it off.
A wild game that ends level, with everyone too tired to be disappointed.
The lead changes hands, then changes back. A point each, and a hundred talking points.
Lclose: They're the better side for long spells, but one lapse is all it takes.
A late goal turns a point into nothing. The away end goes quiet; the home end explodes.
Close. So close. Close doesn't go on the table.
Lbig: It unravels quickly. Every mistake is punished and the heads drop long before the end.
A heavy defeat. There is nowhere to hide on a night like this.
By the hour mark it's about damage limitation. They don't limit much.

injured: {J} watches from the stands, his leg strapped.
{J} spends the match in the stands with a hood up, wincing at every tackle.
Injured, {J} watches on a TV in the physio room, kicking every ball with his good leg.
suspended: {J} serves his suspension in a club tracksuit in the stands.
Suspended, {J} watches from the directors' box and hates every minute of it.
{J} sits out the match, banned. The longest ninety minutes of his week.

red: Then the red card: a lunge he regrets mid-air.
A second yellow for a tug he didn't need to make. Off he goes.
Straight red — a moment of madness that he will replay all night.
yellow: He picks up a yellow card along the way.
A booking for a cynical foul, the kind managers secretly like.
He's booked for dissent, which annoys him more than the foul would have.

motm: He is named man of the match.
The sponsors hand him the man-of-the-match trophy, which is enormous and slightly ugly.
Man of the match. He gives the trophy to the kit man's son.
The stadium announcer reads his name as man of the match and the crowd roars.

good: He makes the centre-backs miserable all game: running in behind, dropping short, never still.
Every time he gets the ball facing goal, the stadium leans forward.
His movement is a nightmare for the defence; they never settle on who should mark him.
He wins three free kicks in dangerous areas just by being too quick for clumsy legs.
bad: He's starved of service and frustrated when he does get it.
Two big chances come and go. He looks at the sky after the second one.
He's caught offside four times and the home fans start counting.
The centre-back has the better of him in the air all afternoon.

good: He finds pockets nobody else sees and keeps the ball moving at the right speed.
He wins the midfield battle through sheer stubbornness.
His passing sets the tempo; when he plays quickly, the whole team plays quickly.
He covers every blade of grass. The GPS data will be ridiculous.
bad: He's bypassed too often, the game happening over his head.
His passes are a fraction slow and the press eats him alive.
He gives the ball away cheaply twice in his own half. The second one nearly costs a goal.
He never finds his rhythm, always half a second behind.

good: He wins every header that matters and reads the danger before it arrives.
One goal-saving block in the second half is worth as much as any goal.
He's calm on the ball and ruthless off it.
The striker he's marking is substituted with twenty minutes left, a quiet admission.
bad: He's turned too easily and the winger enjoys himself.
One misjudged header leads to a big chance; the keeper saves him.
He looks nervous with the ball at his feet and the crowd senses it.
Caught on the wrong side of his man more than once.

good: He makes two saves that he has no business making.
He commands his box like he owns it, plucking crosses out of the air.
His distribution starts attack after attack.
One reflex stop in the last minute is the moment of the match.
bad: He flaps at a cross and the defence has to scramble.
A shot he should hold squirms under him.
He's beaten at his near post, the goalkeeper's cardinal sin.
His kicking is erratic and the defence stops trusting him.

good: {Mf} in the press conference: "{J} was excellent. He's earning everything he's getting."
"I'm pleased with {J}. He did exactly what we asked and more," says {Mf}.
{Mf} singles him out: "That's the level. Now he does it again next week."
mid: {Mf}: "A good result. Some players can give more, but we take the win."
"Three points. The rest we fix on Monday," {Mf} tells reporters.
bad: {Mf} won't be drawn on {J}: "We won. That's what matters today."
"Not everyone was at their level," says {Mf}. Everyone knows who he means.
none: {Mf} praises the squad: "Everybody contributed, on and off the pitch."
"A team performance," says {Mf}, which is what managers say when they're happy.

good: {Mf}: "{J} was one of the positives. We should have won."
"I can't fault {J}'s attitude," says {Mf}. "The result, I can fault."
mid: "A point. We wanted three," says {Mf}, through slightly clenched teeth.
{Mf}: "We move on. There are things to improve."
bad: {Mf} is asked about {J}'s display and takes a long breath before answering: "He knows he can do more."
"Some decisions today were not good enough," says {Mf}. {J} reads the quote on the bus.

good: {Mf}: "Even in defeat, {J} showed character."
"If everyone had {J}'s attitude today, we don't lose," says {Mf}. It doesn't go down well in the dressing room.
mid: "We lost the details," says {Mf}. "Football is details."
{Mf} keeps it short: "Not good enough. Collectively."
bad: {Mf} is blunt: "Some players were not ready for this game." He doesn't need to name {J}.
"We need more from certain players," says {Mf}. The cameras find {J} on the bench.
none: {Mf}: "A painful day. We look at ourselves first."
"No excuses," says {Mf}, and then gives three.

W: In the dressing room the music goes up and {CAPl} does a dance nobody asked for.
The bus home is loud. Somebody orders {FOOD} for forty people.
Ice baths have never felt so pleasant.
D: The dressing room is flat. Nobody can decide whether to be happy or annoyed, so everyone is both.
Quiet showers, quick exits. A point is a point.
{CAPl} gives a short speech. It's about next week.
L: The dressing room is silent except for the sound of tape being peeled off ankles.
On the bus, every phone is face-down. Nobody wants to read anything.

high: The dressing room is {J}'s place now. He sits next to {T}, the jokes go through him, and younger players ask his opinion.
{J} has become part of the furniture of this squad — the good kind. When he's quiet, people notice and ask why.
The lads have nicknamed him something unprintable and affectionate. It means he belongs.
{CAP} asks {J} to help organise the squad's end-of-month dinner. It's a small thing. It isn't small.
mid: The dressing room is neither warm nor cold. {J} has his little group around {T}, and polite nods for everyone else.
{J} is still working out the invisible rules of this dressing room: who sits where, who talks first, who never gets teased.
A normal week in the dressing room: a prank involving shin pads, an argument about music, a fine for being late.
The squad tolerates him, likes him, maybe. It's a work in progress.
low: Conversations stop when {J} walks into the dressing room. It might be paranoia. It might not.
{J} changes in silence. A clique around {R} laughs at something on a phone and glances his way.
Nobody passes him the aux cable. Nobody asks how his weekend was. Small things. Heavy things.
{CAP} tells him, kindly but clearly, that some of the boys think he's 'not one of us'.
ally: {T} has become a real friend: rides to training, shared playlists, an unspoken agreement to have each other's back.
{T} invites {J} round for dinner with his family. The kids climb all over him.
{T} defends {J} in a heated team meeting. It's noticed.
rival: Things with {R} are frosty. A shoulder in training here, a pointed silence there.
{R} makes a joke about {J}'s last game in front of the whole squad. A few laugh.
{J} and {R} go for the same ball in a training game and neither pulls out. The coaches separate them.

high: Home feels warm this week. {MUM}'s voice notes arrive every morning, half prayer and half instructions to eat properly.
{DAD} watches every match now, even the boring ones, and texts tactical advice that is always wrong and always welcome.
{SIB} has a photo of {J} as {SIBhis} phone wallpaper and pretends it's ironic.
A box arrives from home: snacks, a hand-knitted thing, a note from {MUM}. The squad steal the snacks.
mid: The calls with home are short this week — everyone is busy, nobody is upset.
{MUM} asks the same three questions she always asks. He gives the same three answers. It's comforting.
{DAD} sends a link to an article about {J} with no message. That's {DAD}.
{SIB} wants advice over video call about something at {SIBplace}. {J} is no help at all.
low: The family group chat has gone quiet, and the silence feels pointed.
{DAD} hasn't called in weeks. {MUM} says he's 'busy'. {J} knows better.
Every call home turns into an argument about something else that is really about the same thing.
He opens the family chat, types a message, deletes it. Types again. Deletes it.

high: With {Pf}, home is the quiet place. She knows when to ask about the match and when to just put the kettle on.
{Pf} has started a tradition: whatever happens on the pitch, they eat {FOOD} together on Sunday night.
{Pf} sends him a voice note before every game. He listens to it in the tunnel.
{J} catches himself planning a future with {Pf} in it. It doesn't scare him.
mid: Things with {Pf} are fine. Busy, but fine. They keep promising each other a proper weekend.
{Pf} is patient with his schedule. Patience isn't infinite, and they both know it.
A small argument about where to eat becomes a long argument about how little time they spend together, then a quiet truce.
{Pf} watches the match from the family section and gives him a thumbs up he can just about see.
low: {Pf} is distant. When he talks about football, her eyes drift to her phone.
The flat is full of unfinished conversations.
{Pf} says 'I'm fine' in the tone that means the opposite, and he's too tired to ask.
Another evening of two people in the same room on two different planets.

single: He's single, and at the moment the only relationship he has time for is with the ice bath.
His teammates keep trying to set him up with someone's cousin. He keeps saying he's focused. Mostly true.
Dating as a young footballer is complicated: nobody knows if people like you or the shirt.
{SIB} keeps asking when he's going to bring someone home. {MUM} pretends not to be listening.

high: The old crew are still the old crew: {BFf}, still {BFjob}, still the funniest person {J} has ever met.
{BFf} sends him memes about his own bad passes. It keeps him humble.
His friends from home don't care about his stats. That's exactly why he needs them.
The group chat named after a joke from years ago is still the most important place in {J}'s phone.
mid: He sees less of his friends than he'd like. {BFf} understands. Mostly.
Life has got busy on both sides. The group chat is quieter, not dead.
{BFf} posts a photo from a party {J} couldn't go to. It stings, a little.
low: {BFf} doesn't reply to messages anymore. The group chat has a new name, and {J} isn't sure he's still in it.
His friends have moved on to new jokes and new places. Fame has made him a guest in his old life.
He realises he hasn't laughed with anyone who isn't paid to be around him in weeks.

abroad: Being abroad means a lot of evenings in a quiet apartment and a lot of time-zone maths before calling home.
He's learning the city slowly: the supermarket, a place to pray, the one restaurant that does rice properly.
The language still trips him up. He orders the same meal every time because he knows how to pronounce it.
Homesickness arrives at strange times: a smell in the street, a song in a shop.

stressHigh: At 2am {J} is awake, scrolling, heart racing for no reason he can name. The pressure has moved into his body.
He grinds his teeth in his sleep now. The club dentist has noticed. So has he.
Everything feels urgent and nothing feels finished. He writes a list of worries just to see them outside his head; the list is long.
His chest is tight before training, and it isn't the fitness test.
moraleLow: Late at night, {J} wonders if he's good enough. It isn't the first time this month.
He looks at old photos of himself at fifteen, grinning in borrowed boots, and doesn't recognise the feeling.
Some nights he thinks about quitting. Then the alarm goes off at seven and he goes to training anyway.
The doubt is quiet but constant, like traffic noise.
moraleHigh: {J} lies in bed grinning at the ceiling like an idiot. Life is good, and he knows it won't always be.
He's happy, properly happy, and it makes him play braver.
Some nights you fall asleep the moment your head hits the pillow because there's nothing to worry about. Tonight is one.
neutral: The week ends. {J} sets his alarm, plugs in his phone, and lets the noise fade.
He writes three lines in the notebook he keeps by the bed: what went well, what didn't, what's next.
Sleep comes slowly, but it comes.
Another week closer to wherever this is going.

arrive: {J} walks into {NEWCLUB}'s training ground for the first time. New badge, new language in the dressing room, new manager: {M}. Everyone is polite. Nobody owes him anything.
First day at {NEWCLUB}. A tour of the facilities, a photo with the shirt, a locker with a stranger's name still half-peeled off it.
{NEWCLUB} welcome him with a press conference, a medical and a dressing room full of people deciding what they think of him.
free: The contract runs out. No farewell ceremony, no banner — just a cleared locker and a phone that has to start ringing.
Free agency. It sounds like freedom. It feels like waiting.
He's a free agent. His agent says 'calls are coming'. His phone says otherwise.

ntDebut: When the anthem plays, {J} sings every word and does not trust himself to look at the stands.
The national shirt feels heavier than any club shirt. {MUM} is crying somewhere in the crowd, he's sure of it.
He thinks of {DAD} teaching him to kick a ball against the wall of their house. Then the whistle goes.

monitoring: The national team's scouts are in the stand this week. {J} is told, and pretends not to care.
His name has appeared on a provisional list. Everyone at home already knows.
called: The call-up arrives by email and then by forty messages from relatives.
National team duty. {MUM} has already bought a new shirt with his name on it.

seasonReflect: He sits on the empty pitch after the last game of the season, the sprinklers going, thinking about all of it.
Another season in the books. He writes down what he learned. The list is longer than last year's.
The season ends and the body sighs. Rest, then start again.
milestoneLine: Numbers like that used to be dreams. Now they're stats.
Somewhere, a fifteen-year-old version of {J} would lose his mind.
